[§](https://docs.rs#get-the-current-time-in-your-systems-time-zone)Get the current time in your system’s time zone

The [ Zoned::now](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.now) returns your system’s time and also attempts
to automatically find your system’s default time zone via

[:](https://docs.rs/tz/struct.TimeZone.html#method.system)

`tz::TimeZone::system````
use jiff::Zoned;
let now = Zoned::now();
println!("{now}");
// Output: 2024-07-10T17:09:28.168146054-04:00[America/New_York]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#print-the-current-time-rounded-to-the-nearest-second)Print the current time rounded to the nearest second

This uses the [ Zoned::round](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.round) API to round a zoned datetime to the nearest
second. This is useful, for example, if you don’t care about fractional
seconds:

```
use jiff::{Unit, Zoned};
let now = Zoned::now().round(Unit::Second)?;
println!("{now}");
// Output: 2024-07-10T17:09:28-04:00[America/New_York]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#print-todays-date-at-a-specific-time)Print today’s date at a specific time

Let’s say you want to get the current date at 2pm. Here’s one way of doing it
that makes use of [ Zoned::with](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.with):

```
use jiff::Zoned;
let zdt = Zoned::now().with()
    .hour(14)
    .minute(0)
    .second(0)
    .subsec_nanosecond(0)
    .build()?;
println!("{zdt}");
// Output: 2024-07-12T14:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]
```
Or, if the time is known to be valid, you can use the infallible
[ civil::time](https://docs.rs/civil/fn.time.html) convenience constructor:

```
use jiff::{civil::time, Zoned};
let zdt = Zoned::now().with().time(time(14, 0, 0, 0)).build()?;
println!("{zdt}");
// Output: 2024-07-12T14:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]
```
You can eliminate the possibility of a panic at runtime by using `time` in
a `const` block:

```
use jiff::{civil::time, Zoned};
let zdt = Zoned::now().with().time(const { time(14, 0, 0, 0) }).build()?;
println!("{zdt}");
// Output: 2024-07-12T14:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#print-the-current-unix-timestamp)Print the current Unix timestamp

This prints a Unix timestamp as the number of seconds since the Unix epoch
via [ Timestamp::now](https://docs.rs/struct.Timestamp.html#method.now):

```
use jiff::Timestamp;
let now = Timestamp::now();
println!("{}", now.as_second());
// Output: 1720646365
```
Or print the current timestamp to nanosecond precision (which is the maximum supported by Jiff):

```
use jiff::Timestamp;
let now = Timestamp::now();
println!("{}", now.as_nanosecond());
// Output: 1720646414218901664
```
[§](https://docs.rs#print-the-datetime-for-a-timestamp)Print the datetime for a timestamp

This example shows how to convert a Unix timestamp, in milliseconds, to
a zoned datetime in the system’s current time zone. This utilizes the
[ Timestamp::from_millisecond](https://docs.rs/struct.Timestamp.html#method.from_millisecond) constructor,

[to get the default time zone and the](https://docs.rs/tz/struct.TimeZone.html#method.system)

`tz::TimeZone::system`[routine to convert a timestamp to a zoned datetime.](https://docs.rs/struct.Timestamp.html#method.to_zoned)

`Timestamp::to_zoned````
use jiff::{tz::TimeZone, Timestamp};
let ts = Timestamp::from_millisecond(1_720_646_365_567)?;
let zdt = ts.to_zoned(TimeZone::system());
println!("{zdt}");
// Output: 2024-07-10T17:19:25.567-04:00[America/New_York]
// Or if you just want the RFC 3339 time without bothering with time zones:
assert_eq!(ts.to_string(), "2024-07-10T21:19:25.567Z");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#create-a-zoned-datetime-from-civil-time)Create a zoned datetime from civil time

This example demonstrates the convenience constructor, [ civil::date](https://docs.rs/civil/fn.date.html),
for a

[. And use the](https://docs.rs/civil/struct.Date.html)

`civil::Date`[method to create a](https://docs.rs/civil/struct.Date.html#method.at)

`civil::Date::at`[. Once we have a civil datetime, we can use](https://docs.rs/civil/struct.DateTime.html)

`civil::DateTime`[to do a time zone lookup and convert it to a precise instant in time:](https://docs.rs/civil/struct.DateTime.html#method.in_tz)

`civil::DateTime::in_tz````
use jiff::civil::date;
let zdt = date(2023, 12, 31).at(18, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2023-12-31T18:30:00-05:00[America/New_York]");
```
Note that [ civil::date](https://docs.rs/civil/fn.date.html) should only be used for inputs that are known to be
correct since it panics for an invalid date. If your date isn’t known to be
valid, then use the fallible

[constructor.](https://docs.rs/civil/struct.Date.html#method.new)

`civil::Date::new`[§](https://docs.rs#change-an-instant-from-one-time-zone-to-another)Change an instant from one time zone to another

This shows how to find the civil time, in New York, when World War 1 ended:

```
use jiff::civil::date;
let zdt1 = date(1918, 11, 11).at(11, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("Europe/Paris")?;
let zdt2 = zdt1.in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(
    zdt2.to_string(),
    "1918-11-11T06:00:00-05:00[America/New_York]",
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#find-the-duration-between-two-zoned-datetimes)Find the duration between two zoned datetimes

This shows how to compute a span between two zoned datetimes. This utilizes
a [ Zoned](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html)’s implementation for

`Sub`, permitting one to subtract two zoned
datetimes via the `-` operator:```
use jiff::civil::date;
let zdt1 = date(2020, 8, 26).at(6, 27, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let zdt2 = date(2023, 12, 31).at(18, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let span = zdt2 - zdt1;
assert_eq!(format!("{span:#}"), "29341h 3m");
```
The above returns no units bigger than hours because it makes the operation
reversible in all cases. But if you don’t need reversibility (i.e., adding the
span returned to `zdt1` gives you `zdt2`), then you can ask for bigger units
via [ Zoned::until](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.until) to make the span more comprehensible:

```
use jiff::{civil::date, Unit};
let zdt1 = date(2020, 8, 26).at(6, 27, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let zdt2 = date(2023, 12, 31).at(18, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let span = zdt1.until((Unit::Year, &zdt2))?;
assert_eq!(format!("{span:#}"), "3y 4mo 5d 12h 3m");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#add-a-duration-to-a-zoned-datetime)Add a duration to a zoned datetime

This example shows how one can add a [ Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html) to a

[via](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html)

`Zoned`[to get a new](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.checked_add)

`Zoned::checked_add``Zoned` value. We utilize the [trait for convenience construction of](https://docs.rs/trait.ToSpan.html)

`ToSpan``Span` values.```
use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan};
let zdt1 = date(2020, 8, 26).at(6, 27, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let span = 3.years().months(4).days(5).hours(12).minutes(3);
let zdt2 = zdt1.checked_add(span)?;
assert_eq!(zdt2.to_string(), "2023-12-31T18:30:00-05:00[America/New_York]");
```
As with [ civil::date](https://docs.rs/civil/fn.date.html), the

[trait should only be used with inputs that are known to be valid. If you aren’t sure whether the inputs are valid, then use](https://docs.rs/trait.ToSpan.html)

`ToSpan`[and its fallible mutators like](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.new)

`Span::new`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.try_years)

`Span::try_years`[§](https://docs.rs#dealing-with-ambiguity)Dealing with ambiguity

In some cases, civil datetimes either don’t exist in a particular time zone or
are repeated. By default, Jiff automatically uses the
[ tz::Disambiguation::Compatible](https://docs.rs/tz/enum.Disambiguation.html#variant.Compatible) strategy for choosing an instant in all
cases:

```
use jiff::civil::date;
// 2:30 on 2024-03-10 in New York didn't exist. It's a "gap."
// The compatible strategy selects the datetime after the gap.
let zdt = date(2024, 3, 10).at(2, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2024-03-10T03:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]");
// 1:30 on 2024-11-03 in New York appeared twice. It's a "fold."
// The compatible strategy selects the datetime before the fold.
let zdt = date(2024, 11, 3).at(1, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2024-11-03T01:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]");
```
For more control over disambiguation, see
[ tz::TimeZone::to_ambiguous_zoned](https://docs.rs/tz/struct.TimeZone.html#method.to_ambiguous_zoned). Or

[if you’re parsing zoned datetimes.](https://docs.rs/fmt/temporal/struct.DateTimeParser.html#method.disambiguation)

`fmt::temporal::DateTimeParser::disambiguation`[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-span)Parsing a span

Jiff supports parsing ISO 8601 duration strings:

```
use jiff::Span;
let span: Span = "P5y1w10dT5h59m".parse()?;
let expected = Span::new().years(5).weeks(1).days(10).hours(5).minutes(59);
assert_eq!(span, expected.fieldwise());
```
The same format is used for serializing and deserializing `Span` values when
the `serde` feature is enabled.

Jiff also supports a bespoke [“friendly” format](https://docs.rs/fmt/friendly/index.html) as
well:

```
use jiff::Span;
let expected = Span::new().years(5).weeks(1).days(10).hours(5).minutes(59);
let span: Span = "5 years, 1 week, 10 days, 5 hours, 59 minutes".parse()?;
assert_eq!(span, expected.fieldwise());
let span: Span = "5yrs 1wk 10d 5hrs 59mins".parse()?;
assert_eq!(span, expected.fieldwise());
let span: Span = "5y 1w 10d 5h 59m".parse()?;
assert_eq!(span, expected.fieldwise());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-an-rfc-2822-datetime-string)Parsing an RFC 2822 datetime string

While you probably shouldn’t pick [RFC 2822](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2822) as a format for new things, it is
sometimes necessary to use it when something else requires it (like HTTP
or email). Parsing and printing of RFC 2822 datetimes is done via the
[ fmt::rfc2822](https://docs.rs/fmt/rfc2822/index.html) module:

```
use jiff::fmt::rfc2822;
let zdt1 = rfc2822::parse("Thu, 29 Feb 2024 05:34 -0500")?;
let zdt2 = zdt1.in_tz("Australia/Tasmania")?;
assert_eq!(rfc2822::to_string(&zdt2)?, "Thu, 29 Feb 2024 21:34:00 +1100");
let zdt3 = zdt1.in_tz("Asia/Kolkata")?;
assert_eq!(rfc2822::to_string(&zdt3)?, "Thu, 29 Feb 2024 16:04:00 +0530");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-strftime-and-strptime-for-formatting-and-parsing)Using `strftime` and `strptime` for formatting and parsing

Jiff has support for the C style [ strftime](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009695399/functions/strftime.html) and

[functions for formatting and parsing datetime types. All of Jiff’s datetime types having a](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009695399/functions/strptime.html)

`strptime``strptime` constructor for parsing, and a `strftime` method for formatting.
For example, this shows how to use [to parsed a string in a “odd” custom format into a zoned datetime:](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.strptime)

`Zoned::strptime````
use jiff::Zoned;
let zdt = Zoned::strptime(
    "%A, %B %d, %Y at %I:%M%p %Q",
    "Monday, July 15, 2024 at 5:30pm US/Eastern",
)?;
assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2024-07-15T17:30:00-04:00[US/Eastern]");
```
And this shows how to use [ Zoned::strftime](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.strftime) to format a zoned datetime.
Note the use of

`%Z`, which will print a time zone abbreviation (when one is
available) instead of an offset (`%Z` can’t be used for parsing):```
use jiff::civil::date;
let zdt = date(2024, 7, 15).at(17, 30, 59, 0).in_tz("Australia/Tasmania")?;
// %-I instead of %I means no padding.
let string = zdt.strftime("%A, %B %d, %Y at %-I:%M%P %Z").to_string();
assert_eq!(string, "Monday, July 15, 2024 at 5:30pm AEST");
```
However, time zone abbreviations aren’t parsable because they are ambiguous.
For example, `CST` can stand for `Central Standard Time`, `Cuba Standard Time`
or `China Standard Time`. Instead, it is recommended to use `%Q` to format an
IANA time zone identifier (which can be parsed, as shown above):

```
use jiff::civil::date;
let zdt = date(2024, 7, 15).at(17, 30, 59, 0).in_tz("Australia/Tasmania")?;
// %-I instead of %I means no padding.
let string = zdt.strftime("%A, %B %d, %Y at %-I:%M%P %Q").to_string();
assert_eq!(string, "Monday, July 15, 2024 at 5:30pm Australia/Tasmania");
```
See the [ fmt::strtime](https://docs.rs/fmt/strtime/index.html) module documentation for supported conversion
specifiers and other APIs.

[§](https://docs.rs#serializing-and-deserializing-integer-timestamps-with-serde)Serializing and deserializing integer timestamps with Serde

Sometimes you need to interact with external services that use integer timestamps
instead of something more civilized like RFC 3339. Since [ Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.Timestamp.html)’s
Serde integration uses RFC 3339, you’ll need to override the default. While
you could hand-write this, Jiff provides convenience routines that do this
for you. But you do need to wire it up via

[Serde’s](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with):

`with` attribute```
use jiff::Timestamp;
#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize, serde::Serialize)]
struct Record {
    #[serde(with = "jiff::fmt::serde::timestamp::second::required")]
    timestamp: Timestamp,
}
let json = r#"{"timestamp":1517644800}"#;
let got: Record = serde_json::from_str(&json)?;
assert_eq!(got.timestamp, Timestamp::from_second(1517644800)?);
assert_eq!(serde_json::to_string(&got)?, json);
```
If you need to support optional timestamps via `Option<Timestamp>`, then use
`jiff::fmt::serde::timestamp::second::optional` instead.

For more, see the [ fmt::serde](https://docs.rs/fmt/serde/index.html) sub-module. (This requires enabling Jiff’s

`serde` crate feature.)[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

[§](https://docs.rs#ecosystem-features)Ecosystem features

- **std**(enabled by default) - When enabled, Jiff will depend on Rust’s standard library. This is needed for things that require interacting with your system, such as reading- `/usr/share/zoneinfo`on Unix systems for time zone information, or for finding your system’s default time zone. But if you don’t need that (or can bundle the Time Zone Database), then Jiff has nearly full functionality without- `std`enabled, excepting things like- `std::error::Error`trait implementations and a global time zone database (which is required for things like- `Timestamp::in_tz`
- **alloc**(enabled by default) - When enabled, Jiff will depend on the- `alloc`crate. In particular, this enables functionality that requires or greatly benefits from dynamic memory allocation. If you can enable this, it is strongly encouraged that you do so. Without it, only fixed time zones are supported and error messages are significantly degraded. Also, the sizes of some types get bigger. If you have use cases for Jiff in a no-std and no-alloc context, I would love feedback on the issue tracker about your use cases.
- **logging**- When enabled, the- `log`crate is used to emit messages where appropriate. Generally speaking, this is reserved for system interaction points, such as finding the system copy of the Time Zone Database or finding the system’s default time zone.
- **serde**- When enabled, all of the datetime and span types in Jiff implement serde’s- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`traits. The format used is specified by Temporal, but it’s a mix of the “best” parts of RFC 3339, RFC 9557 and ISO 8601. See the- `fmt::temporal`
- **js**- On- *only*the- `wasm32-unknown-unknown`and- `wasm64-unknown-unknown`targets, the- `js`feature will add dependencies on- `js-sys`and- `wasm-bindgen`. These dependencies are used to determine the current datetime and time zone from the web browser. On these targets without the- `js`feature enabled, getting the current datetime will panic (because that’s what- `std::time::SystemTime::now()`does), and it won’t be possible to determine the time zone. This feature is disabled by default because not all uses of- `wasm{32,64}-unknown-unknown`are in a web context, although- *many*are (for example, when using- `wasm-pack`). Only binary, tests and benchmarks should enable this feature. See- [Platform support](https://docs.rs/_documentation/platform/index.html)for more details.
- **defmt**- When enabled, Jiff will implement the- `defmt::Format`- `core::fmt`machinery is not practical to use. Note that, at time of writing (2026-06-12), not all public types in this crate implement- `defmt::Format`- `defmt`support but don’t have it in Jiff, then please- [open a new issue](https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/new).

[§](https://docs.rs#time-zone-features)Time zone features

- **tz-system**(enabled by default) - When enabled, Jiff will include code that attempts to determine the “system” time zone. For example, on Unix systems, this is usually determined by looking at the symlink information on- `/etc/localtime`. But in general, it’s very platform specific and heuristic oriented.
- **tz-fat**(enabled by default) - When enabled, Jiff will “fatten” time zone data with extra transitions to make time zone lookups faster. This may result in increased heap memory (when loading time zones from- `/usr/share/zoneinfo`) or increased binary size (when using the- `jiff-static`proc macros). Note that this doesn’t add more transitions than are likely already in- `/usr/share/zoneinfo`, depending on how it was generated.
- **tzdb-bundle-always**- When enabled, Jiff will forcefully depend on the- `jiff-tzdb`crate, which embeds an entire copy of the Time Zone Database. You should avoid this unless you have a specific need for it, since it is better to rely on your system’s copy of time zone information. (Which may be updated multiple times per year.)
- **tzdb-bundle-platform**(enabled by default) - When enabled, Jiff will depend on- `jiff-tzdb`only for platforms where it is known that there is no canonical copy of the Time Zone Database. For example, Windows.
- **tzdb-zoneinfo**(enabled by default) - When enabled, Jiff will attempt to look for your system’s copy of the Time Zone Database.
- **tzdb-concatenated**(enabled by default) - When enabled, Jiff will attempt to look for a system copy of the- [Concatenated Time Zone Database](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/libcore/+/jb-mr2-release/luni/src/main/java/libcore/util/ZoneInfoDB.java). This is primarily meant for reading time zone information on Android platforms. The- `ANDROID_ROOT`and- `ANDROID_DATA`environment variables (with sensible default fallbacks) are used to construct candidate paths to look for this database. For more on this, see the- [Android section of the platform support documentation](https://docs.rs/_documentation/platform/index.html#android).
- **static**- When enabled, new procedural macros will be added to the- `tz`sub-module for creating static- `TimeZone`values at compile-time. This adds a dependency on- `jiff-static`- `jiff-tzdb`- `jiff-static`defines the macros, and Jiff re-exports them. This also enables- `static-tz`.
- **static-tz**- When enabled, a- `jiff::tz::include`procedural macro will become available. This takes a TZif file path, like- `/usr/share/zoneinfo/Israel`, as input and returns a- `TimeZone`value at compile time.

[§](https://docs.rs#performance-features)Performance features

- **perf-inline**(enabled by default) - When enabled, a number of- `inline(always)`annotations are used inside of Jiff to improve performance. This can especially impact formatting and parsing of datetimes. If the extra performance isn’t needed or if you want to prioritize smaller binary sizes and shorter compilation times over runtime performance, then it can be useful to disable this feature.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/jiff/0.2.31/src/jiff/lib.rs.html

# jiff/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)/*!
[2](https://docs.rs#2)Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit
[3](https://docs.rs#3)of success. The focus of this library is providing high level datetime
[4](https://docs.rs#4)primitives that are difficult to misuse and have reasonable performance.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)
[6](https://docs.rs#6)Jiff takes enormous inspiration from [Temporal], which is a [TC39] proposal to
[7](https://docs.rs#7)improve datetime handling in JavaScript.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)
[9](https://docs.rs#9)Here is a quick example that shows how to parse a typical RFC 3339 instant,
[10](https://docs.rs#10)convert it to a zone aware datetime, add a span of time and losslessly print
[11](https://docs.rs#11)it:
[12](https://docs.rs#12)
[13](https://docs.rs#13)```
[14](https://docs.rs#14)use jiff::{Timestamp, ToSpan};
[15](https://docs.rs#15)
[16](https://docs.rs#16)let time: Timestamp = "2024-07-11T01:14:00Z".parse()?;
[17](https://docs.rs#17)let zoned = time.in_tz("America/New_York")?.checked_add(1.month().hours(2))?;
[18](https://docs.rs#18)assert_eq!(zoned.to_string(), "2024-08-10T23:14:00-04:00[America/New_York]");
[19](https://docs.rs#19)// Or, if you want an RFC3339 formatted string:
[20](https://docs.rs#20)assert_eq!(zoned.timestamp().to_string(), "2024-08-11T03:14:00Z");
[21](https://docs.rs#21)
[22](https://docs.rs#22)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[23](https://docs.rs#23)```
[24](https://docs.rs#24)
[25](https://docs.rs#25)[TC39]: https://tc39.es/
[26](https://docs.rs#26)[Temporal]: https://tc39.es/proposal-temporal/docs/index.html
[27](https://docs.rs#27)
[28](https://docs.rs#28)# Overview
[29](https://docs.rs#29)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)The primary type in this crate is [`Zoned`]. A `Zoned` value is a datetime that
[31](https://docs.rs#31)corresponds to a precise instant in time in a particular geographic region.
[32](https://docs.rs#32)Users of this crate may find it helpful to think of a `Zoned` as a triple of
[33](https://docs.rs#33)the following components:
[34](https://docs.rs#34)
[35](https://docs.rs#35)* A [`Timestamp`] is a 96-bit integer of nanoseconds since the [Unix epoch].
[36](https://docs.rs#36)A timestamp is a precise instant in time.
[37](https://docs.rs#37)* A [`civil::DateTime`] is an inexact calendar date and clock time. The terms
[38](https://docs.rs#38)"civil", "local", "plain" and "naive" are all used in various places to
[39](https://docs.rs#39)describe this same concept.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)* A [`tz::TimeZone`] is a set of rules for determining the civil time, via an
[41](https://docs.rs#41)offset from [UTC], in a particular geographic region.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)
[43](https://docs.rs#43)All three of these components are used to provide convenient high level
[44](https://docs.rs#44)operations on `Zoned` such as computing durations, adding durations and
[45](https://docs.rs#45)rounding.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)
[47](https://docs.rs#47)A [`Span`] is this crate's primary duration type. It mixes calendar and clock
[48](https://docs.rs#48)units into a single type. Jiff also provides [`SignedDuration`], which is like
[49](https://docs.rs#49)[`std::time::Duration`], but signed. Users should default to a `Span` for
[50](https://docs.rs#50)representing durations when using Jiff.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)
[52](https://docs.rs#52)[Unix epoch]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time
[53](https://docs.rs#53)[UTC]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time
[54](https://docs.rs#54)
[55](https://docs.rs#55)The remainder of this documentation is organized as follows:
[56](https://docs.rs#56)
[57](https://docs.rs#57)* [Features](#features) gives a very brief summary of the features Jiff does
[58](https://docs.rs#58)and does not support.
[59](https://docs.rs#59)* [Usage](#usage) shows how to add Jiff to your Rust project.
[60](https://docs.rs#60)* [Examples](#examples) shows a small cookbook of programs for common tasks.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)* [Crate features](#crate-features) documents the Cargo features that can be
[62](https://docs.rs#62)enabled or disabled for this crate.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)
[64](https://docs.rs#64)Also, the `_documentation` sub-module serves to provide longer form
[65](https://docs.rs#65)documentation:
[66](https://docs.rs#66)
[67](https://docs.rs#67)* [Comparison with other Rust datetime crates](crate::_documentation::comparison)
[68](https://docs.rs#68)* [The API design rationale for Jiff](crate::_documentation::design)
[69](https://docs.rs#69)* [Platform support](crate::_documentation::platform)
[70](https://docs.rs#70)* [CHANGELOG](crate::_documentation::changelog)
[71](https://docs.rs#71)
[72](https://docs.rs#72)# Features
[73](https://docs.rs#73)
[74](https://docs.rs#74)Here is a non-exhaustive list of the things that Jiff supports:
[75](https://docs.rs#75)
[76](https://docs.rs#76)* Automatic and seamless integration with your system's copy of the
[77](https://docs.rs#77)[IANA Time Zone Database]. When a platform doesn't have a time zone database,
[78](https://docs.rs#78)Jiff automatically embeds a copy of it.
[79](https://docs.rs#79)* A separation of datetime types between absolute times ([`Timestamp`] and
[80](https://docs.rs#80)[`Zoned`]) and civil times ([`civil::DateTime`]).
[81](https://docs.rs#81)* Nanosecond precision.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)* Time zone and daylight saving time aware arithmetic.
[83](https://docs.rs#83)* The primary duration type, [`Span`], mixes calendar and clock
[84](https://docs.rs#84)units to provide an all-in-one human friendly experience that is time zone
[85](https://docs.rs#85)aware.
[86](https://docs.rs#86)* An "absolute" duration type, [`SignedDuration`], is like
[87](https://docs.rs#87)[`std::time::Duration`] but signed.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)* Datetime rounding.
[89](https://docs.rs#89)* Span rounding, including calendar units and including taking time zones into
[90](https://docs.rs#90)account.
[91](https://docs.rs#91)* Formatting and parsing datetimes via a Temporal-specified hybrid format
[92](https://docs.rs#92)that takes the best parts of [RFC 3339], [RFC 9557] and [ISO 8601]. This
[93](https://docs.rs#93)includes lossless round tripping of zone aware datetimes and durations.
[94](https://docs.rs#94)* Formatting and parsing according to [RFC 2822].
[95](https://docs.rs#95)* Formatting and parsing via routines similar to [`strftime`] and [`strptime`].
[96](https://docs.rs#96)* Formatting and parsing durations via a bespoke
[97](https://docs.rs#97)["friendly" format](crate::fmt::friendly), with Serde support, that is meant
[98](https://docs.rs#98)to service the [`humantime`](https://docs.rs/humantime) use cases.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)* Opt-in Serde integration.
[100](https://docs.rs#100)* Full support for dealing with ambiguous civil datetimes.
[101](https://docs.rs#101)* Protection against deserializing datetimes in the future with an offset
[102](https://docs.rs#102)different than what is possible with your copy of the Time Zone Database.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)(This is done via [`tz::OffsetConflict`].)
[104](https://docs.rs#104)* APIs that panic by design are clearly documented as such and few in number.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)Otherwise, all operations that can fail, including because of overflow,
[106](https://docs.rs#106)return a `Result`.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)
[108](https://docs.rs#108)Here is also a list of things that Jiff doesn't currently support, along with
[109](https://docs.rs#109)a link to a relevant issue (if one exists).
[110](https://docs.rs#110)
[111](https://docs.rs#111)* [Leap seconds]. (Jiff will automatically constrain times like `23:59:60` to
[112](https://docs.rs#112)`23:59:59`.)
[113](https://docs.rs#113)* Time scales other than Unix.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)* [Calendars other than Gregorian].
[115](https://docs.rs#115)* [Localization].
[116](https://docs.rs#116)* [Changing the representation size, precision or limits on the minimum and
[117](https://docs.rs#117)maximum datetime values.][cppchrono]
[118](https://docs.rs#118)* [Jiff aims to have reasonable performance and may not be capable of doing the
[119](https://docs.rs#119)fastest possible thing.][perf]
[120](https://docs.rs#120)
[121](https://docs.rs#121)At present, it is recommended to use the [`icu`] crate via [`jiff-icu`] for
[122](https://docs.rs#122)localization and non-Gregorian use cases.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)
[124](https://docs.rs#124)[Leap seconds]: https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/7
[125](https://docs.rs#125)[Calendars other than Gregorian]: https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/6
[126](https://docs.rs#126)[Localization]: https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/4
[127](https://docs.rs#127)[cppchrono]: https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/3
[128](https://docs.rs#128)[perf]: https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/17
[129](https://docs.rs#129)[`icu`]: https://docs.rs/icu
[130](https://docs.rs#130)[`jiff-icu`]: https://docs.rs/jiff-icu
[131](https://docs.rs#131)
[132](https://docs.rs#132)Please file an issue if you can think of more (substantial) things to add to
[133](https://docs.rs#133)the above list.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)
[135](https://docs.rs#135)[IANA Time Zone Database]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tz_database
[136](https://docs.rs#136)[RFC 3339]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339
[137](https://docs.rs#137)[RFC 9557]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9557.html
[138](https://docs.rs#138)[ISO 8601]: https://www.iso.org/iso-8601-date-and-time-format.html
[139](https://docs.rs#139)
[140](https://docs.rs#140)# Usage
[141](https://docs.rs#141)
[142](https://docs.rs#142)Jiff is [on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/jiff) and can be
[143](https://docs.rs#143)used by adding `jiff` to your dependencies in your project's `Cargo.toml`.
[144](https://docs.rs#144)Or more simply, just run `cargo add jiff`.
[145](https://docs.rs#145)
[146](https://docs.rs#146)Here is a complete example that creates a new Rust project, adds a dependency
[147](https://docs.rs#147)on `jiff`, creates the source code for a simple datetime program and then runs
[148](https://docs.rs#148)it.
[149](https://docs.rs#149)
[150](https://docs.rs#150)First, create the project in a new directory:
[151](https://docs.rs#151)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)```text
[153](https://docs.rs#153)$ cargo new jiff-example
[154](https://docs.rs#154)$ cd jiff-example
[155](https://docs.rs#155)```
[156](https://docs.rs#156)
[157](https://docs.rs#157)Second, add a dependency on `jiff`:
[158](https://docs.rs#158)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)```text
[160](https://docs.rs#160)$ cargo add jiff
[161](https://docs.rs#161)```
[162](https://docs.rs#162)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)Third, edit `src/main.rs`. Delete what's there and replace it with this:
[164](https://docs.rs#164)
[165](https://docs.rs#165)```
[166](https://docs.rs#166)use jiff::{Unit, Zoned};
[167](https://docs.rs#167)
[168](https://docs.rs#168)fn main() -> Result<(), jiff::Error> {
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    let now = Zoned::now().round(Unit::Second)?;
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    println!("{now}");
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    Ok(())
[172](https://docs.rs#172)}
[173](https://docs.rs#173)```
[174](https://docs.rs#174)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)Fourth, run it with `cargo run`:
[176](https://docs.rs#176)
[177](https://docs.rs#177)```text
[178](https://docs.rs#178)$ cargo run
[179](https://docs.rs#179)   Compiling jiff v0.2.0 (/home/andrew/rust/jiff)
[180](https://docs.rs#180)   Compiling jiff-play v0.2.0 (/home/andrew/tmp/scratch/rust/jiff-play)
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 1.37s
[182](https://docs.rs#182)     Running `target/debug/jiff-play`
[183](https://docs.rs#183)2024-07-10T19:54:20-04:00[America/New_York]
[184](https://docs.rs#184)```
[185](https://docs.rs#185)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)The first time you run the program will show more output like above. But
[187](https://docs.rs#187)subsequent runs shouldn't have to re-compile the dependencies.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)

[206](https://docs.rs#206)### Get the current time in your system's time zone
[207](https://docs.rs#207)
[208](https://docs.rs#208)The [`Zoned::now`] returns your system's time and also attempts
[209](https://docs.rs#209)to automatically find your system's default time zone via
[210](https://docs.rs#210)[`tz::TimeZone::system`]:
[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)```
[213](https://docs.rs#213)use jiff::Zoned;
[214](https://docs.rs#214)
[215](https://docs.rs#215)let now = Zoned::now();
[216](https://docs.rs#216)println!("{now}");
[217](https://docs.rs#217)// Output: 2024-07-10T17:09:28.168146054-04:00[America/New_York]
[218](https://docs.rs#218)```
[219](https://docs.rs#219)
[220](https://docs.rs#220)### Print the current time rounded to the nearest second
[221](https://docs.rs#221)
[222](https://docs.rs#222)This uses the [`Zoned::round`] API to round a zoned datetime to the nearest
[223](https://docs.rs#223)second. This is useful, for example, if you don't care about fractional
[224](https://docs.rs#224)seconds:
[225](https://docs.rs#225)
[226](https://docs.rs#226)```
[227](https://docs.rs#227)use jiff::{Unit, Zoned};
[228](https://docs.rs#228)
[229](https://docs.rs#229)let now = Zoned::now().round(Unit::Second)?;
[230](https://docs.rs#230)println!("{now}");
[231](https://docs.rs#231)// Output: 2024-07-10T17:09:28-04:00[America/New_York]
[232](https://docs.rs#232)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[233](https://docs.rs#233)```
[234](https://docs.rs#234)
[235](https://docs.rs#235)### Print today's date at a specific time
[236](https://docs.rs#236)
[237](https://docs.rs#237)Let's say you want to get the current date at 2pm. Here's one way of doing it
[238](https://docs.rs#238)that makes use of [`Zoned::with`]:
[239](https://docs.rs#239)
[240](https://docs.rs#240)```
[241](https://docs.rs#241)use jiff::Zoned;
[242](https://docs.rs#242)
[243](https://docs.rs#243)let zdt = Zoned::now().with()
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    .hour(14)
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    .minute(0)
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    .second(0)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    .subsec_nanosecond(0)
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    .build()?;
[249](https://docs.rs#249)println!("{zdt}");
[250](https://docs.rs#250)// Output: 2024-07-12T14:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]
[251](https://docs.rs#251)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[252](https://docs.rs#252)```
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)Or, if the time is known to be valid, you can use the infallible
[255](https://docs.rs#255)[`civil::time`](civil::time()) convenience constructor:
[256](https://docs.rs#256)
[257](https://docs.rs#257)```
[258](https://docs.rs#258)use jiff::{civil::time, Zoned};
[259](https://docs.rs#259)
[260](https://docs.rs#260)let zdt = Zoned::now().with().time(time(14, 0, 0, 0)).build()?;
[261](https://docs.rs#261)println!("{zdt}");
[262](https://docs.rs#262)// Output: 2024-07-12T14:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]
[263](https://docs.rs#263)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[264](https://docs.rs#264)```
[265](https://docs.rs#265)
[266](https://docs.rs#266)You can eliminate the possibility of a panic at runtime by using `time` in
[267](https://docs.rs#267)a `const` block:
[268](https://docs.rs#268)
[269](https://docs.rs#269)```
[270](https://docs.rs#270)use jiff::{civil::time, Zoned};
[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)let zdt = Zoned::now().with().time(const { time(14, 0, 0, 0) }).build()?;
[273](https://docs.rs#273)println!("{zdt}");
[274](https://docs.rs#274)// Output: 2024-07-12T14:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]
[275](https://docs.rs#275)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[276](https://docs.rs#276)```
[277](https://docs.rs#277)
[278](https://docs.rs#278)### Print the current Unix timestamp
[279](https://docs.rs#279)
[280](https://docs.rs#280)This prints a Unix timestamp as the number of seconds since the Unix epoch
[281](https://docs.rs#281)via [`Timestamp::now`]:
[282](https://docs.rs#282)
[283](https://docs.rs#283)```
[284](https://docs.rs#284)use jiff::Timestamp;
[285](https://docs.rs#285)
[286](https://docs.rs#286)let now = Timestamp::now();
[287](https://docs.rs#287)println!("{}", now.as_second());
[288](https://docs.rs#288)// Output: 1720646365
[289](https://docs.rs#289)```
[290](https://docs.rs#290)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)Or print the current timestamp to nanosecond precision (which is the maximum
[292](https://docs.rs#292)supported by Jiff):
[293](https://docs.rs#293)
[294](https://docs.rs#294)```
[295](https://docs.rs#295)use jiff::Timestamp;
[296](https://docs.rs#296)
[297](https://docs.rs#297)let now = Timestamp::now();
[298](https://docs.rs#298)println!("{}", now.as_nanosecond());
[299](https://docs.rs#299)// Output: 1720646414218901664
[300](https://docs.rs#300)```
[301](https://docs.rs#301)
[302](https://docs.rs#302)### Print the datetime for a timestamp
[303](https://docs.rs#303)
[304](https://docs.rs#304)This example shows how to convert a Unix timestamp, in milliseconds, to
[305](https://docs.rs#305)a zoned datetime in the system's current time zone. This utilizes the
[306](https://docs.rs#306)[`Timestamp::from_millisecond`] constructor, [`tz::TimeZone::system`] to get
[307](https://docs.rs#307)the default time zone and the [`Timestamp::to_zoned`] routine to convert a
[308](https://docs.rs#308)timestamp to a zoned datetime.
[309](https://docs.rs#309)
[310](https://docs.rs#310)```
[311](https://docs.rs#311)use jiff::{tz::TimeZone, Timestamp};
[312](https://docs.rs#312)
[313](https://docs.rs#313)let ts = Timestamp::from_millisecond(1_720_646_365_567)?;
[314](https://docs.rs#314)let zdt = ts.to_zoned(TimeZone::system());
[315](https://docs.rs#315)println!("{zdt}");
[316](https://docs.rs#316)// Output: 2024-07-10T17:19:25.567-04:00[America/New_York]
[317](https://docs.rs#317)// Or if you just want the RFC 3339 time without bothering with time zones:
[318](https://docs.rs#318)assert_eq!(ts.to_string(), "2024-07-10T21:19:25.567Z");
[319](https://docs.rs#319)
[320](https://docs.rs#320)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[321](https://docs.rs#321)```
[322](https://docs.rs#322)
[323](https://docs.rs#323)### Create a zoned datetime from civil time
[324](https://docs.rs#324)
[325](https://docs.rs#325)This example demonstrates the convenience constructor, [`civil::date`],
[326](https://docs.rs#326)for a [`civil::Date`]. And use the [`civil::Date::at`] method to create
[327](https://docs.rs#327)a [`civil::DateTime`]. Once we have a civil datetime, we can use
[328](https://docs.rs#328)[`civil::DateTime::in_tz`] to do a time zone lookup and convert it to a precise
[329](https://docs.rs#329)instant in time:
[330](https://docs.rs#330)
[331](https://docs.rs#331)```
[332](https://docs.rs#332)use jiff::civil::date;
[333](https://docs.rs#333)
[334](https://docs.rs#334)let zdt = date(2023, 12, 31).at(18, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
[335](https://docs.rs#335)assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2023-12-31T18:30:00-05:00[America/New_York]");
[336](https://docs.rs#336)
[337](https://docs.rs#337)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[338](https://docs.rs#338)```
[339](https://docs.rs#339)
[340](https://docs.rs#340)Note that [`civil::date`] should only be used for inputs that are known to be
[341](https://docs.rs#341)correct since it panics for an invalid date. If your date isn't known to be
[342](https://docs.rs#342)valid, then use the fallible [`civil::Date::new`] constructor.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)### Change an instant from one time zone to another
[345](https://docs.rs#345)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)This shows how to find the civil time, in New York, when World War 1 ended:
[347](https://docs.rs#347)
[348](https://docs.rs#348)```
[349](https://docs.rs#349)use jiff::civil::date;
[350](https://docs.rs#350)
[351](https://docs.rs#351)let zdt1 = date(1918, 11, 11).at(11, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("Europe/Paris")?;
[352](https://docs.rs#352)let zdt2 = zdt1.in_tz("America/New_York")?;
[353](https://docs.rs#353)assert_eq!(
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    zdt2.to_string(),
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    "1918-11-11T06:00:00-05:00[America/New_York]",
[356](https://docs.rs#356));
[357](https://docs.rs#357)
[358](https://docs.rs#358)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[359](https://docs.rs#359)```
[360](https://docs.rs#360)
[361](https://docs.rs#361)### Find the duration between two zoned datetimes
[362](https://docs.rs#362)
[363](https://docs.rs#363)This shows how to compute a span between two zoned datetimes. This utilizes
[364](https://docs.rs#364)a [`Zoned`]'s implementation for `Sub`, permitting one to subtract two zoned
[365](https://docs.rs#365)datetimes via the `-` operator:
[366](https://docs.rs#366)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)```
[368](https://docs.rs#368)use jiff::civil::date;
[369](https://docs.rs#369)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)let zdt1 = date(2020, 8, 26).at(6, 27, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
[371](https://docs.rs#371)let zdt2 = date(2023, 12, 31).at(18, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
[372](https://docs.rs#372)let span = zdt2 - zdt1;
[373](https://docs.rs#373)assert_eq!(format!("{span:#}"), "29341h 3m");
[374](https://docs.rs#374)
[375](https://docs.rs#375)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[376](https://docs.rs#376)```
[377](https://docs.rs#377)
[378](https://docs.rs#378)The above returns no units bigger than hours because it makes the operation
[379](https://docs.rs#379)reversible in all cases. But if you don't need reversibility (i.e., adding the
[380](https://docs.rs#380)span returned to `zdt1` gives you `zdt2`), then you can ask for bigger units
[381](https://docs.rs#381)via [`Zoned::until`] to make the span more comprehensible:
[382](https://docs.rs#382)
[383](https://docs.rs#383)```
[384](https://docs.rs#384)use jiff::{civil::date, Unit};
[385](https://docs.rs#385)
[386](https://docs.rs#386)let zdt1 = date(2020, 8, 26).at(6, 27, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
[387](https://docs.rs#387)let zdt2 = date(2023, 12, 31).at(18, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
[388](https://docs.rs#388)let span = zdt1.until((Unit::Year, &zdt2))?;
[389](https://docs.rs#389)assert_eq!(format!("{span:#}"), "3y 4mo 5d 12h 3m");
[390](https://docs.rs#390)
[391](https://docs.rs#391)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[392](https://docs.rs#392)```
[393](https://docs.rs#393)
[394](https://docs.rs#394)### Add a duration to a zoned datetime
[395](https://docs.rs#395)
[396](https://docs.rs#396)This example shows how one can add a [`Span`] to a [`Zoned`] via
[397](https://docs.rs#397)[`Zoned::checked_add`] to get a new `Zoned` value. We utilize the [`ToSpan`]
[398](https://docs.rs#398)trait for convenience construction of `Span` values.
[399](https://docs.rs#399)
[400](https://docs.rs#400)```
[401](https://docs.rs#401)use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan};
[402](https://docs.rs#402)
[403](https://docs.rs#403)let zdt1 = date(2020, 8, 26).at(6, 27, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
[404](https://docs.rs#404)let span = 3.years().months(4).days(5).hours(12).minutes(3);
[405](https://docs.rs#405)let zdt2 = zdt1.checked_add(span)?;
[406](https://docs.rs#406)assert_eq!(zdt2.to_string(), "2023-12-31T18:30:00-05:00[America/New_York]");
[407](https://docs.rs#407)
[408](https://docs.rs#408)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[409](https://docs.rs#409)```
[410](https://docs.rs#410)
[411](https://docs.rs#411)As with [`civil::date`], the [`ToSpan`] trait should only be used with inputs
[412](https://docs.rs#412)that are known to be valid. If you aren't sure whether the inputs are valid,
[413](https://docs.rs#413)then use [`Span::new`] and its fallible mutators like [`Span::try_years`].
[414](https://docs.rs#414)
[415](https://docs.rs#415)### Dealing with ambiguity
[416](https://docs.rs#416)
[417](https://docs.rs#417)In some cases, civil datetimes either don't exist in a particular time zone or
[418](https://docs.rs#418)are repeated. By default, Jiff automatically uses the
[419](https://docs.rs#419)[`tz::Disambiguation::Compatible`] strategy for choosing an instant in all
[420](https://docs.rs#420)cases:
[421](https://docs.rs#421)
[422](https://docs.rs#422)```
[423](https://docs.rs#423)use jiff::civil::date;
[424](https://docs.rs#424)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)// 2:30 on 2024-03-10 in New York didn't exist. It's a "gap."
[426](https://docs.rs#426)// The compatible strategy selects the datetime after the gap.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)let zdt = date(2024, 3, 10).at(2, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
[428](https://docs.rs#428)assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2024-03-10T03:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]");
[429](https://docs.rs#429)
[430](https://docs.rs#430)// 1:30 on 2024-11-03 in New York appeared twice. It's a "fold."
[431](https://docs.rs#431)// The compatible strategy selects the datetime before the fold.
[432](https://docs.rs#432)let zdt = date(2024, 11, 3).at(1, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
[433](https://docs.rs#433)assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2024-11-03T01:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]");
[434](https://docs.rs#434)
[435](https://docs.rs#435)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[436](https://docs.rs#436)```
[437](https://docs.rs#437)
[438](https://docs.rs#438)For more control over disambiguation, see
[439](https://docs.rs#439)[`tz::TimeZone::to_ambiguous_zoned`]. Or
[440](https://docs.rs#440)[`fmt::temporal::DateTimeParser::disambiguation`]
[441](https://docs.rs#441)if you're parsing zoned datetimes.
[442](https://docs.rs#442)
[443](https://docs.rs#443)### Parsing a span
[444](https://docs.rs#444)
[445](https://docs.rs#445)Jiff supports parsing ISO 8601 duration strings:
[446](https://docs.rs#446)
[447](https://docs.rs#447)```
[448](https://docs.rs#448)use jiff::Span;
[449](https://docs.rs#449)
[450](https://docs.rs#450)let span: Span = "P5y1w10dT5h59m".parse()?;
[451](https://docs.rs#451)let expected = Span::new().years(5).weeks(1).days(10).hours(5).minutes(59);
[452](https://docs.rs#452)assert_eq!(span, expected.fieldwise());
[453](https://docs.rs#453)
[454](https://docs.rs#454)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[455](https://docs.rs#455)```
[456](https://docs.rs#456)
[457](https://docs.rs#457)The same format is used for serializing and deserializing `Span` values when
[458](https://docs.rs#458)the `serde` feature is enabled.
[459](https://docs.rs#459)
[460](https://docs.rs#460)Jiff also supports a bespoke ["friendly" format](crate::fmt::friendly) as
[461](https://docs.rs#461)well:
[462](https://docs.rs#462)
[463](https://docs.rs#463)```
[464](https://docs.rs#464)use jiff::Span;
[465](https://docs.rs#465)
[466](https://docs.rs#466)let expected = Span::new().years(5).weeks(1).days(10).hours(5).minutes(59);
[467](https://docs.rs#467)let span: Span = "5 years, 1 week, 10 days, 5 hours, 59 minutes".parse()?;
[468](https://docs.rs#468)assert_eq!(span, expected.fieldwise());
[469](https://docs.rs#469)let span: Span = "5yrs 1wk 10d 5hrs 59mins".parse()?;
[470](https://docs.rs#470)assert_eq!(span, expected.fieldwise());
[471](https://docs.rs#471)let span: Span = "5y 1w 10d 5h 59m".parse()?;
[472](https://docs.rs#472)assert_eq!(span, expected.fieldwise());
[473](https://docs.rs#473)
[474](https://docs.rs#474)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[475](https://docs.rs#475)```
[476](https://docs.rs#476)
[477](https://docs.rs#477)### Parsing an RFC 2822 datetime string
[478](https://docs.rs#478)
[479](https://docs.rs#479)While you probably shouldn't pick [RFC 2822] as a format for new things, it is
[480](https://docs.rs#480)sometimes necessary to use it when something else requires it (like HTTP
[481](https://docs.rs#481)or email). Parsing and printing of RFC 2822 datetimes is done via the
[482](https://docs.rs#482)[`fmt::rfc2822`] module:
[483](https://docs.rs#483)
[484](https://docs.rs#484)```
[485](https://docs.rs#485)use jiff::fmt::rfc2822;
[486](https://docs.rs#486)
[487](https://docs.rs#487)let zdt1 = rfc2822::parse("Thu, 29 Feb 2024 05:34 -0500")?;
[488](https://docs.rs#488)let zdt2 = zdt1.in_tz("Australia/Tasmania")?;
[489](https://docs.rs#489)assert_eq!(rfc2822::to_string(&zdt2)?, "Thu, 29 Feb 2024 21:34:00 +1100");
[490](https://docs.rs#490)let zdt3 = zdt1.in_tz("Asia/Kolkata")?;
[491](https://docs.rs#491)assert_eq!(rfc2822::to_string(&zdt3)?, "Thu, 29 Feb 2024 16:04:00 +0530");
[492](https://docs.rs#492)
[493](https://docs.rs#493)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[494](https://docs.rs#494)```
[495](https://docs.rs#495)
[496](https://docs.rs#496)[RFC 2822]: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2822
[497](https://docs.rs#497)
[498](https://docs.rs#498)### Using `strftime` and `strptime` for formatting and parsing
[499](https://docs.rs#499)
[500](https://docs.rs#500)Jiff has support for the C style [`strftime`] and [`strptime`] functions for
[501](https://docs.rs#501)formatting and parsing datetime types. All of Jiff's datetime types having a
[502](https://docs.rs#502)`strptime` constructor for parsing, and a `strftime` method for formatting.
[503](https://docs.rs#503)For example, this shows how to use [`Zoned::strptime`] to parsed a string in
[504](https://docs.rs#504)a "odd" custom format into a zoned datetime:
[505](https://docs.rs#505)
[506](https://docs.rs#506)```
[507](https://docs.rs#507)use jiff::Zoned;
[508](https://docs.rs#508)
[509](https://docs.rs#509)let zdt = Zoned::strptime(
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    "%A, %B %d, %Y at %I:%M%p %Q",
[511](https://docs.rs#511)    "Monday, July 15, 2024 at 5:30pm US/Eastern",
[512](https://docs.rs#512))?;
[513](https://docs.rs#513)assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2024-07-15T17:30:00-04:00[US/Eastern]");
[514](https://docs.rs#514)
[515](https://docs.rs#515)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[516](https://docs.rs#516)```
[517](https://docs.rs#517)
[518](https://docs.rs#518)And this shows how to use [`Zoned::strftime`] to format a zoned datetime.
[519](https://docs.rs#519)Note the use of `%Z`, which will print a time zone abbreviation (when one is
[520](https://docs.rs#520)available) instead of an offset (`%Z` can't be used for parsing):
[521](https://docs.rs#521)
[522](https://docs.rs#522)```
[523](https://docs.rs#523)use jiff::civil::date;
[524](https://docs.rs#524)
[525](https://docs.rs#525)let zdt = date(2024, 7, 15).at(17, 30, 59, 0).in_tz("Australia/Tasmania")?;
[526](https://docs.rs#526)// %-I instead of %I means no padding.
[527](https://docs.rs#527)let string = zdt.strftime("%A, %B %d, %Y at %-I:%M%P %Z").to_string();
[528](https://docs.rs#528)assert_eq!(string, "Monday, July 15, 2024 at 5:30pm AEST");
[529](https://docs.rs#529)
[530](https://docs.rs#530)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[531](https://docs.rs#531)```
[532](https://docs.rs#532)
[533](https://docs.rs#533)However, time zone abbreviations aren't parsable because they are ambiguous.
[534](https://docs.rs#534)For example, `CST` can stand for `Central Standard Time`, `Cuba Standard Time`
[535](https://docs.rs#535)or `China Standard Time`. Instead, it is recommended to use `%Q` to format an
[536](https://docs.rs#536)IANA time zone identifier (which can be parsed, as shown above):
[537](https://docs.rs#537)
[538](https://docs.rs#538)```
[539](https://docs.rs#539)use jiff::civil::date;
[540](https://docs.rs#540)
[541](https://docs.rs#541)let zdt = date(2024, 7, 15).at(17, 30, 59, 0).in_tz("Australia/Tasmania")?;
[542](https://docs.rs#542)// %-I instead of %I means no padding.
[543](https://docs.rs#543)let string = zdt.strftime("%A, %B %d, %Y at %-I:%M%P %Q").to_string();
[544](https://docs.rs#544)assert_eq!(string, "Monday, July 15, 2024 at 5:30pm Australia/Tasmania");
[545](https://docs.rs#545)
[546](https://docs.rs#546)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[547](https://docs.rs#547)```
[548](https://docs.rs#548)
[549](https://docs.rs#549)See the [`fmt::strtime`] module documentation for supported conversion
[550](https://docs.rs#550)specifiers and other APIs.
[551](https://docs.rs#551)
[552](https://docs.rs#552)[`strftime`]: https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009695399/functions/strftime.html
[553](https://docs.rs#553)[`strptime`]: https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009695399/functions/strptime.html
[554](https://docs.rs#554)
[555](https://docs.rs#555)### Serializing and deserializing integer timestamps with Serde
[556](https://docs.rs#556)
[557](https://docs.rs#557)Sometimes you need to interact with external services that use integer timestamps
[558](https://docs.rs#558)instead of something more civilized like RFC 3339. Since [`Timestamp`]'s
[559](https://docs.rs#559)Serde integration uses RFC 3339, you'll need to override the default. While
[560](https://docs.rs#560)you could hand-write this, Jiff provides convenience routines that do this
[561](https://docs.rs#561)for you. But you do need to wire it up via [Serde's `with` attribute]:
[562](https://docs.rs#562)
[563](https://docs.rs#563)```
[564](https://docs.rs#564)use jiff::Timestamp;
[565](https://docs.rs#565)
[566](https://docs.rs#566)#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize, serde::Serialize)]
[567](https://docs.rs#567)struct Record {
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    #[serde(with = "jiff::fmt::serde::timestamp::second::required")]
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    timestamp: Timestamp,
[570](https://docs.rs#570)}
[571](https://docs.rs#571)
[572](https://docs.rs#572)let json = r#"{"timestamp":1517644800}"#;
[573](https://docs.rs#573)let got: Record = serde_json::from_str(&json)?;
[574](https://docs.rs#574)assert_eq!(got.timestamp, Timestamp::from_second(1517644800)?);
[575](https://docs.rs#575)assert_eq!(serde_json::to_string(&got)?, json);
[576](https://docs.rs#576)
[577](https://docs.rs#577)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[578](https://docs.rs#578)```
[579](https://docs.rs#579)
[580](https://docs.rs#580)If you need to support optional timestamps via `Option<Timestamp>`, then use
[581](https://docs.rs#581)`jiff::fmt::serde::timestamp::second::optional` instead.
[582](https://docs.rs#582)
[583](https://docs.rs#583)For more, see the [`fmt::serde`] sub-module. (This requires enabling Jiff's
[584](https://docs.rs#584)`serde` crate feature.)
[585](https://docs.rs#585)
[586](https://docs.rs#586)[Serde's `with` attribute]: https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with
[587](https://docs.rs#587)
[588](https://docs.rs#588)# Crate features
[589](https://docs.rs#589)
[590](https://docs.rs#590)### Ecosystem features
[591](https://docs.rs#591)
[592](https://docs.rs#592)* **std** (enabled by default) -
[593](https://docs.rs#593)  When enabled, Jiff will depend on Rust's standard library. This is needed
[594](https://docs.rs#594)  for things that require interacting with your system, such as reading
[595](https://docs.rs#595)  `/usr/share/zoneinfo` on Unix systems for time zone information, or for
[596](https://docs.rs#596)  finding your system's default time zone. But if you don't need that (or can
[597](https://docs.rs#597)  bundle the Time Zone Database), then Jiff has nearly full functionality
[598](https://docs.rs#598)  without `std` enabled, excepting things like `std::error::Error` trait
[599](https://docs.rs#599)  implementations and a global time zone database (which is required for
[600](https://docs.rs#600)  things like [`Timestamp::in_tz`] to work).
[601](https://docs.rs#601)* **alloc** (enabled by default) -
[602](https://docs.rs#602)  When enabled, Jiff will depend on the `alloc` crate. In particular, this
[603](https://docs.rs#603)  enables functionality that requires or greatly benefits from dynamic memory
[604](https://docs.rs#604)  allocation. If you can enable this, it is strongly encouraged that you do so.
[605](https://docs.rs#605)  Without it, only fixed time zones are supported and error messages are
[606](https://docs.rs#606)  significantly degraded. Also, the sizes of some types get bigger. If you
[607](https://docs.rs#607)  have use cases for Jiff in a no-std and no-alloc context, I would love
[608](https://docs.rs#608)  feedback on the issue tracker about your use cases.
[609](https://docs.rs#609)* **logging** -
[610](https://docs.rs#610)  When enabled, the `log` crate is used to emit messages where appropriate.
[611](https://docs.rs#611)  Generally speaking, this is reserved for system interaction points, such as
[612](https://docs.rs#612)  finding the system copy of the Time Zone Database or finding the system's
[613](https://docs.rs#613)  default time zone.
[614](https://docs.rs#614)* **serde** -
[615](https://docs.rs#615)  When enabled, all of the datetime and span types in Jiff implement
[616](https://docs.rs#616)  serde's `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits. The format used is specified by
[617](https://docs.rs#617)  Temporal, but it's a mix of the "best" parts of RFC 3339, RFC 9557 and
[618](https://docs.rs#618)  ISO 8601. See the [`fmt::temporal`] module for more details on the format
[619](https://docs.rs#619)  used.
[620](https://docs.rs#620)* **js** -
[621](https://docs.rs#621)  On _only_ the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `wasm64-unknown-unknown` targets,
[622](https://docs.rs#622)  the `js` feature will add dependencies on `js-sys` and `wasm-bindgen`.
[623](https://docs.rs#623)  These dependencies are used to determine the current datetime and time
[624](https://docs.rs#624)  zone from the web browser. On these targets without the `js` feature
[625](https://docs.rs#625)  enabled, getting the current datetime will panic (because that's what
[626](https://docs.rs#626)  `std::time::SystemTime::now()` does), and it won't be possible to determine
[627](https://docs.rs#627)  the time zone. This feature is disabled by default because not all uses
[628](https://docs.rs#628)  of `wasm{32,64}-unknown-unknown` are in a web context, although _many_ are
[629](https://docs.rs#629)  (for example, when using `wasm-pack`). Only binary, tests and benchmarks
[630](https://docs.rs#630)  should enable this feature. See
[631](https://docs.rs#631)  [Platform support](crate::_documentation::platform) for more details.
[632](https://docs.rs#632)* **defmt** -
[633](https://docs.rs#633)  When enabled, Jiff will implement the [`defmt::Format`] trait for many
[634](https://docs.rs#634)  of its types. This is useful for embedded environments where the usual
[635](https://docs.rs#635)  `core::fmt` machinery is not practical to use. Note that, at time of writing
[636](https://docs.rs#636)  (2026-06-12), not all public types in this crate implement [`defmt::Format`].
[637](https://docs.rs#637)  If there are types for which you need `defmt` support but don't have it in
[638](https://docs.rs#638)  Jiff, then please [open a new issue][issue-new].
[639](https://docs.rs#639)
[640](https://docs.rs#640)### Time zone features
[641](https://docs.rs#641)
[642](https://docs.rs#642)* **tz-system** (enabled by default) -
[643](https://docs.rs#643)  When enabled, Jiff will include code that attempts to determine the "system"
[644](https://docs.rs#644)  time zone. For example, on Unix systems, this is usually determined by
[645](https://docs.rs#645)  looking at the symlink information on `/etc/localtime`. But in general, it's
[646](https://docs.rs#646)  very platform specific and heuristic oriented.
[647](https://docs.rs#647)* **tz-fat** (enabled by default) -
[648](https://docs.rs#648)  When enabled, Jiff will "fatten" time zone data with extra transitions to
[649](https://docs.rs#649)  make time zone lookups faster. This may result in increased heap memory
[650](https://docs.rs#650)  (when loading time zones from `/usr/share/zoneinfo`) or increased binary
[651](https://docs.rs#651)  size (when using the `jiff-static` proc macros). Note that this doesn't add
[652](https://docs.rs#652)  more transitions than are likely already in `/usr/share/zoneinfo`, depending
[653](https://docs.rs#653)  on how it was generated.
[654](https://docs.rs#654)* **tzdb-bundle-always** -
[655](https://docs.rs#655)  When enabled, Jiff will forcefully depend on the `jiff-tzdb` crate, which
[656](https://docs.rs#656)  embeds an entire copy of the Time Zone Database. You should avoid this unless
[657](https://docs.rs#657)  you have a specific need for it, since it is better to rely on your system's
[658](https://docs.rs#658)  copy of time zone information. (Which may be updated multiple times per
[659](https://docs.rs#659)  year.)
[660](https://docs.rs#660)* **tzdb-bundle-platform** (enabled by default) -
[661](https://docs.rs#661)  When enabled, Jiff will depend on `jiff-tzdb` only for platforms where it is
[662](https://docs.rs#662)  known that there is no canonical copy of the Time Zone Database. For example,
[663](https://docs.rs#663)  Windows.
[664](https://docs.rs#664)* **tzdb-zoneinfo** (enabled by default) -
[665](https://docs.rs#665)  When enabled, Jiff will attempt to look for your system's copy of the Time
[666](https://docs.rs#666)  Zone Database.
[667](https://docs.rs#667)* **tzdb-concatenated** (enabled by default) -
[668](https://docs.rs#668)  When enabled, Jiff will attempt to look for a system copy of the
[669](https://docs.rs#669)  [Concatenated Time Zone Database]. This is primarily meant for reading time
[670](https://docs.rs#670)  zone information on Android platforms. The `ANDROID_ROOT` and `ANDROID_DATA`
[671](https://docs.rs#671)  environment variables (with sensible default fallbacks) are used to construct
[672](https://docs.rs#672)  candidate paths to look for this database. For more on this, see the
[673](https://docs.rs#673)  [Android section of the platform support documentation](crate::_documentation::platform#android).
[674](https://docs.rs#674)* **static** -
[675](https://docs.rs#675)  When enabled, new procedural macros will be added to the `tz` sub-module for
[676](https://docs.rs#676)  creating static `TimeZone` values at compile-time. This adds a dependency on
[677](https://docs.rs#677)  [`jiff-static`] and [`jiff-tzdb`]. `jiff-static` defines the macros, and Jiff
[678](https://docs.rs#678)  re-exports them. This also enables `static-tz`.
[679](https://docs.rs#679)* **static-tz** -
[680](https://docs.rs#680)  When enabled, a `jiff::tz::include` procedural macro will become available.
[681](https://docs.rs#681)  This takes a TZif file path, like `/usr/share/zoneinfo/Israel`, as input and
[682](https://docs.rs#682)  returns a `TimeZone` value at compile time.
[683](https://docs.rs#683)
[684](https://docs.rs#684)### Performance features
[685](https://docs.rs#685)
[686](https://docs.rs#686)* **perf-inline** (enabled by default) -
[687](https://docs.rs#687)  When enabled, a number of `inline(always)` annotations are used inside of
[688](https://docs.rs#688)  Jiff to improve performance. This can especially impact formatting and
[689](https://docs.rs#689)  parsing of datetimes. If the extra performance isn't needed or if you want
[690](https://docs.rs#690)  to prioritize smaller binary sizes and shorter compilation times over
[691](https://docs.rs#691)  runtime performance, then it can be useful to disable this feature.
[692](https://docs.rs#692)
[693](https://docs.rs#693)[`jiff-static`]: https://docs.rs/jiff-static
[694](https://docs.rs#694)[`jiff-tzdb`]: https://docs.rs/jiff-tzdb
[695](https://docs.rs#695)[Concatenated Time Zone Database]: https://android.googlesource.com/platform/libcore/+/jb-mr2-release/luni/src/main/java/libcore/util/ZoneInfoDB.java
[696](https://docs.rs#696)[issue-new]: https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff/issues/new

# Zoned in jiff - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jiff/0.2.31/jiff/struct.Zoned.html

`pub struct Zoned { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A time zone aware instant in time.

A `Zoned` value can be thought of as the combination of following types,
all rolled into one:

- A `Timestamp`
- A `DateTime`
- A `TimeZone`

In particular, a `Zoned` is specifically designed for dealing with
datetimes in a time zone aware manner. Here are some highlights:

- Arithmetic automatically adjusts for daylight saving time (DST), using
the rules defined by [RFC 5545](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5545).
- Creating new `Zoned`values from other`Zoned`values via`Zoned::with``02:30`) can do so without worrying that the time will be invalid due to DST transitions.
- An approximate superset of the `DateTime``Zoned`, but where each of its operations take time zone into account when appropriate. For example,`DateTime::start_of_day``Zoned::start_of_day`
- When using a `Zoned`, it is easy to switch between civil datetime (the day you see on the calendar and the time you see on the clock) and Unix time (a precise instant in time). Indeed, a`Zoned`can be losslessy converted to any other datetime type in this crate:`Timestamp``DateTime``Date``Time`
- A `Zoned`value can be losslessly serialized and deserialized, via[serde](https://serde.rs/), by adhering to[RFC 8536](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8536). An example of a serialized zoned datetime is`2024-07-04T08:39:00-04:00[America/New_York]`.
- Since a `Zoned`stores a`TimeZone`

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-and-printing)Parsing and printing

The `Zoned` type provides convenient trait implementations of
[ std::str::FromStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html) and

[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)

`std::fmt::Display````
use jiff::Zoned;
let zdt: Zoned = "2024-06-19 15:22[America/New_York]".parse()?;
// Notice that the second component and the offset have both been added.
assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2024-06-19T15:22:00-04:00[America/New_York]");
// While in the above case the datetime is unambiguous, in some cases, it
// can be ambiguous. In these cases, an offset is required to correctly
// roundtrip a zoned datetime. For example, on 2024-11-03 in New York, the
// 1 o'clock hour was repeated twice, corresponding to the end of daylight
// saving time.
//
// So because of the ambiguity, this time could be in offset -04 (the first
// time 1 o'clock is on the clock) or it could be -05 (the second time
// 1 o'clock is on the clock, corresponding to the end of DST).
//
// By default, parsing uses a "compatible" strategy for resolving all cases
// of ambiguity: in forward transitions (gaps), the later time is selected.
// And in backward transitions (folds), the earlier time is selected.
let zdt: Zoned = "2024-11-03 01:30[America/New_York]".parse()?;
// As we can see, since this was a fold, the earlier time was selected
// because the -04 offset is the first time 1 o'clock appears on the clock.
assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2024-11-03T01:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]");
// But if we changed the offset and re-serialized, the only thing that
// changes is, indeed, the offset. This demonstrates that the offset is
// key to ensuring lossless serialization.
let zdt = zdt.with().offset(jiff::tz::offset(-5)).build()?;
assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2024-11-03T01:30:00-05:00[America/New_York]");
```
A `Zoned` can also be parsed from just a time zone aware date (but the
time zone annotation is still required). In this case, the time is set to
midnight:

```
use jiff::Zoned;
let zdt: Zoned = "2024-06-19[America/New_York]".parse()?;
assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2024-06-19T00:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]");
// ... although it isn't always midnight, in the case of a time zone
// transition at midnight!
let zdt: Zoned = "2015-10-18[America/Sao_Paulo]".parse()?;
assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2015-10-18T01:00:00-02:00[America/Sao_Paulo]");
```
For more information on the specific format supported, see the
[ fmt::temporal](https://docs.rs/fmt/temporal/index.html) module documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#default-value)Default value

For convenience, this type implements the `Default` trait. Its default
value corresponds to `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000000` in the special UTC
time zone. That is, it is the Unix epoch. One can also access this value
via the [ Zoned::UNIX_EPOCH](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#associatedconstant.UNIX_EPOCH) constant.

[§](https://docs.rs#leap-seconds)Leap seconds

Jiff does not support leap seconds. Jiff behaves as if they don’t exist.
The only exception is that if one parses a datetime with a second component
of `60`, then it is automatically constrained to `59`:

```
use jiff::{civil::date, Zoned};
let zdt: Zoned = "2016-12-31 23:59:60[Australia/Tasmania]".parse()?;
assert_eq!(zdt.datetime(), date(2016, 12, 31).at(23, 59, 59, 0));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#comparisons)Comparisons

The `Zoned` type provides both `Eq` and `Ord` trait implementations to
facilitate easy comparisons. When a zoned datetime `zdt1` occurs before a
zoned datetime `zdt2`, then `zdt1 < zdt2`. For example:

```
use jiff::civil::date;
let zdt1 = date(2024, 3, 11).at(1, 25, 15, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let zdt2 = date(2025, 1, 31).at(0, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert!(zdt1 < zdt2);
```
Note that `Zoned` comparisons only consider the precise instant in time.
The civil datetime or even the time zone are completely ignored. So it’s
possible for a zoned datetime to be less than another even if it’s civil
datetime is bigger:

```
use jiff::civil::date;
let zdt1 = date(2024, 7, 4).at(12, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let zdt2 = date(2024, 7, 4).at(11, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/Los_Angeles")?;
assert!(zdt1 < zdt2);
// But if we only compare civil datetime, the result is flipped:
assert!(zdt1.datetime() > zdt2.datetime());
```
The same applies for equality as well. Two `Zoned` values are equal, even
if they have different time zones, when the instant in time is identical:

```
use jiff::civil::date;
let zdt1 = date(2024, 7, 4).at(12, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let zdt2 = date(2024, 7, 4).at(9, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/Los_Angeles")?;
assert_eq!(zdt1, zdt2);
```
(Note that this is different from
[Temporal’s  ZonedDateTime.equals](https://tc39.es/proposal-temporal/docs/zoneddatetime.html#equals) comparison, which will
take time zone into account for equality. This is because

`Eq` and `Ord`
trait implementations must be consistent in Rust. If you need Temporal’s
behavior, then use `zdt1 == zdt2 && zdt1.time_zone() == zdt2.time_zone()`.)[§](https://docs.rs#arithmetic)Arithmetic

This type provides routines for adding and subtracting spans of time, as
well as computing the span of time between two `Zoned` values. These
operations take time zones into account.

For adding or subtracting spans of time, one can use any of the following routines:

- `Zoned::checked_add`- `Zoned::checked_sub`
- `Zoned::saturating_add`- `Zoned::saturating_sub`

Additionally, checked arithmetic is available via the `Add` and `Sub`
trait implementations. When the result overflows, a panic occurs.

```
use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan};
let start = date(2024, 2, 25).at(15, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
// `Zoned` doesn't implement `Copy`, so you'll want to use `&start` instead
// of `start` if you want to keep using it after arithmetic.
let one_week_later = start + 1.weeks();
assert_eq!(one_week_later.datetime(), date(2024, 3, 3).at(15, 45, 0, 0));
```
One can compute the span of time between two zoned datetimes using either
[ Zoned::until](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.until) or

[. It’s also possible to subtract two](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.since)

`Zoned::since``Zoned` values directly via a `Sub` trait implementation:```
use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan};
let zdt1 = date(2024, 5, 3).at(23, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let zdt2 = date(2024, 2, 25).at(7, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(zdt1 - zdt2, 1647.hours().minutes(30).fieldwise());
```
The `until` and `since` APIs are polymorphic and allow re-balancing and
rounding the span returned. For example, the default largest unit is hours
(as exemplified above), but we can ask for bigger units:

```
use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan, Unit};
let zdt1 = date(2024, 5, 3).at(23, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let zdt2 = date(2024, 2, 25).at(7, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(
    zdt1.since((Unit::Year, &zdt2))?,
    2.months().days(7).hours(16).minutes(30).fieldwise(),
);
```
Or even round the span returned:

```
use jiff::{civil::date, RoundMode, ToSpan, Unit, ZonedDifference};
let zdt1 = date(2024, 5, 3).at(23, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let zdt2 = date(2024, 2, 25).at(7, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(
    zdt1.since(
        ZonedDifference::new(&zdt2)
            .smallest(Unit::Day)
            .largest(Unit::Year),
    )?,
    2.months().days(7).fieldwise(),
);
// `ZonedDifference` uses truncation as a rounding mode by default,
// but you can set the rounding mode to break ties away from zero:
assert_eq!(
    zdt1.since(
        ZonedDifference::new(&zdt2)
            .smallest(Unit::Day)
            .largest(Unit::Year)
            .mode(RoundMode::HalfExpand),
    )?,
    // Rounds up to 8 days.
    2.months().days(8).fieldwise(),
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rounding)Rounding

A `Zoned` can be rounded based on a [ ZonedRound](https://docs.rs/struct.ZonedRound.html) configuration of
smallest units, rounding increment and rounding mode. Here’s an example
showing how to round to the nearest third hour:

```
use jiff::{civil::date, Unit, ZonedRound};
let zdt = date(2024, 6, 19)
    .at(16, 27, 29, 999_999_999)
    .in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(
    zdt.round(ZonedRound::new().smallest(Unit::Hour).increment(3))?,
    date(2024, 6, 19).at(15, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?,
);
// Or alternatively, make use of the `From<(Unit, i64)> for ZonedRound`
// trait implementation:
assert_eq!(
    zdt.round((Unit::Hour, 3))?,
    date(2024, 6, 19).at(15, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?,
);
```
See [ Zoned::round](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.round) for more details.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jiff/zoned.rs.html#396-401)#### pub const [UNIX_EPOCH](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.UNIX_EPOCH): [Zoned](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jiff/zoned.rs.html#396-401)

#### pub const [UNIX_EPOCH](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.UNIX_EPOCH): [Zoned](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html)

The Unix epoch represented as a timestamp in the [ UTC](https://docs.rs/tz/struct.TimeZone.html#associatedconstant.UTC)
time zone.

The Unix epoch corresponds to the instant at `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z`.

This is equivalent to
`Zoned::new(Timestamp::UNIX_EPOCH, TimeZone::UTC)`. This is also
equivalent to `Zoned::default()`, but it can be used in a `const`
context.

Returns the current system time in this system’s time zone.

If the system’s time zone could not be found, then
[ TimeZone::unknown](https://docs.rs/tz/struct.TimeZone.html#method.unknown) is used instead. When this happens, a

`WARN`
level log message will be emitted. (To see it, one will need to install
a logger that is compatible with the `log` crate and enable Jiff’s
`logging` Cargo feature.)To create a `Zoned` value for the current time in a particular
time zone other than the system default time zone, use
`Timestamp::now().to_zoned(time_zone)`. In particular, using
[ Timestamp::now](https://docs.rs/struct.Timestamp.html#method.now) avoids the work required to fetch the system time
zone if you did

`Zoned::now().with_time_zone(time_zone)`.[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This panics if the system clock is set to a time value outside of the
range `-009999-01-01T00:00:00Z..=9999-12-31T11:59:59.999999999Z`. The
justification here is that it is reasonable to expect the system clock
to be set to a somewhat sane, if imprecise, value.

If you want to get the current Unix time fallibly, use
[ Zoned::try_from](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.try_from) with a

`std::time::SystemTime` as input.This may also panic when `SystemTime::now()` itself panics. The most
common context in which this happens is on the `wasm32-unknown-unknown`
target. If you’re using that target in the context of the web (for
example, via `wasm-pack`), and you’re an application, then you should
enable Jiff’s `js` feature. This will automatically instruct Jiff in
this very specific circumstance to execute JavaScript code to determine
the current time from the web browser.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use jiff::{Timestamp, Zoned};
assert!(Zoned::now().timestamp() > Timestamp::UNIX_EPOCH);
```
Creates a new `Zoned` value from a specific instant in a particular
time zone. The time zone determines how to render the instant in time
into civil time. (Also known as “clock,” “wall,” “local” or “naive”
time.)

To create a new zoned datetime from another with a particular field
value, use the methods on [ ZonedWith](https://docs.rs/struct.ZonedWith.html) via

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Zoned.html#method.with)

`Zoned::with`[§](https://docs.rs#construction-from-civil-time)Construction from civil time

A `Zoned` value can also be created from a civil time via the following
methods:

- `DateTime::in_tz`
- `DateTime::to_zoned`- `TimeZone`.
- `Date::in_tz`
- `Date::to_zoned`- `TimeZone`and attempts to use midnight as the clock time.

Whenever one is converting from civil time to a zoned
datetime, it is possible for the civil time to be ambiguous.
That is, it might be a clock reading that could refer to
multiple possible instants in time, or it might be a clock
reading that never exists. The above routines will use a
[ Disambiguation::Compatible](https://docs.rs/tz/enum.Disambiguation.html#variant.Compatible)
strategy to automatically resolve these corner cases.

If one wants to control how ambiguity is resolved (including
by returning an error), use [ TimeZone::to_ambiguous_zoned](https://docs.rs/tz/struct.TimeZone.html#method.to_ambiguous_zoned)
and select the desired strategy via a method on

[.](https://docs.rs/tz/struct.AmbiguousZoned.html)

`AmbiguousZoned`[§](https://docs.rs#example-what-was-the-civil-time-in-tasmania-at-the-unix-epoch)Example: What was the civil time in Tasmania at the Unix epoch?

```
use jiff::{tz::TimeZone, Timestamp, Zoned};
let tz = TimeZone::get("Australia/Tasmania")?;
let zdt = Zoned::new(Timestamp::UNIX_EPOCH, tz);
assert_eq!(
    zdt.to_string(),
    "1970-01-01T11:00:00+11:00[Australia/Tasmania]",
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-what-was-the-civil-time-in-new-york-when-world-war-1-ended)Example: What was the civil time in New York when World War 1 ended?

```
use jiff::civil::date;
let zdt1 = date(1918, 11, 11).at(11, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("Europe/Paris")?;
let zdt2 = zdt1.in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(
    zdt2.to_string(),
    "1918-11-11T06:00:00-05:00[America/New_York]",
